Thank you to everyone involved in helping get the release of War out.  Stuff like the manual, label and box are things that stopped me from originally distributing it back in 2007.  I'm excited to see it finally being so close to distribution.

** Teaser Alert **
Back when I was finishing War, I had another idea for a Bally homebrew.  I started doing some proof of concept code and artwork for it, and if it looks like we have the means to produce more carts after War, I may move forward on it once again.  I won't go into details about what the game is, but here is some info about it.

- It's another port of an arcade game.  Yeah I know a lot of people want to see an original.
- It will be nearly impossible to play via an emulator.  You'll need the Bally controllers and real hardware.
- It will have music/better sound than War.  This is a weak spot of mine but will work on it for this game.

I also had a couple ideas of original games.  These would come later if we had the ability to produce carts and there was interest.  The Astrocade is very fun to program and I'd like to do more.  It's potential was rarely tapped from the original library of games.

Mike G.

> >>
> Playing Galaxian or Space Invaders on an Apple never seems to have the same spirit of the arcade game. The controls seem sluggish and the action seems slower.

>

> The difference [between computers with slow or fast graphics], then, is not in the display, but in the use of dedicated chip sets and a Z80 to supervise those chips.

>

> "We've done marketing surveys on [Robby Roto] and it has the same attraction as "Pac Man," said game designer Bob Ogden. "In fact, Pac Man players prefer it."
> >>

>

8507:
I just spent about forty-five minutes looking through the boxes in the garage that I'd hoped would contain the five pre-Arcadian newsletters called "Arcadians." 

The story has ups and downs:

1) Good news - Bob was pretty good about keeping everything in labeled folders.

2) Bad news - The boxes have been shifted around and nothing is in quite the right order it should be in.

3) Good news - I found five separate folders labeled "Arcadians" 1-5!

4) Bad news - Each "Arcadians" folder was completely empty!

That doesn't mean the newsletters aren't in those boxes, but it does dash my hopes quite a bit.  There is just SO much paperwork to look through.  The only way that I can expect to find them now is by accident.

Here are some neat finds on my recent perusal of "The Fabris Collection:"

1) Viper Systems Hardware - I found two high-quality 8x10 glossy ORIGINAL pictures of the Viper that I've not seen before.  I think that this was when they were designing the  add-under in 1983/84.  There is a picture of the outside of the computer and the inside (and all the chips are quite easy to see... and they're are a lot of them).  This is pretty neat and is high on my agenda to scan-- but not yet.

2) ZGrass-32 - I found a glossy, high-quality version of the Z-Grass 32.  This is the very picture that I was asking just a few days ago where the original came from.  All this time I've had one!

3) A letter from Brett Bilbrey - In 1981 (or was it '82?) Brett (and a whole bunch of other people) wrote to Bob saying that they were willing to field test the add-under.  I guess that Bob must have asked about this in the Arcadian.  Brett, you never tested a unit, right?  Do you know if any such test occurred?

4) Partial Disassembly of Star Battle - This is a partial disassembly of, I think, the WORST cartridge game on the Astrocade.  This disassembly was done by Tom Wood, who did a LOT of disassembly work that is in the Bob Fabris collection.  Unfortunately he concentrated on stuff that we have the ACTUAL source code for (like BASIC and the ROM).  It seems like a LOT of work... but it all went to a good cause.  In October of 1978 (VERY early!) Tom went wrote a booklet that explained how to use many of the on-board ROM subroutines.  I've only seen the booklet in Bob's collection, but I've seen the booklet, in slightly modified form, as a booklet by The Cursor Group.

5) Peek & Poke Manual - I found an original of this manual that was mentioned a few days ago.  It's the same one that I have... someplace.  Fred's name has been crossed-out and Brett's name has been written in its place.  I'm under the impression that Fred DID write the book, but that he got all of his information from Brett.  Correct?

I won't be scanning ANYTHING until everything that is currently on my hard drive and not yet on the website has been added.  That shouldn't actually take too much longer.  The bulk of it is now up.  Mostly I have the 120 archived BASIC programs to add to the website.  I usually test all the 2000-BAUD programs, just to make sure that I can load them.  So, I can't just put them online yet.

Looking through "The Fabris Collection" is rewarding, but a little overwhelming.  I know that I'll eventually get it all online, but it's going to take SO many years to do.  Still, as a said in a recent posting, it's fun to do.  Sometimes I open a folder and I'll see something that I've never seen or even HEARD of before.

Adam

One thing I don't understand though. If the unit has  32K(and it does), 
why does the switch that switches the first 8K into cart space labeled 
6K/2K?

This is a direct carry-over from the Blue Ram. The Utility takes your program and loads it down to !6000 (6000 hex)
Then when you throw the switch, the Lil' WHITE RAM diverts the !4000 line (A14) so that the Bally thinks it's !2000, where the cartridge resides. The main problem with doing it this way is that the Utility clobbers itself AND Blue Ram BASIC's variable area, so both have to be reloaded each time. Leroy Flamm got real tired of loading the Utility from tape each time, so he wrote the program that is listed on Bally Alley. Once he figured out how to do this, he was able to design the "BASIC cart" as we know it. The major stumbling block he had pertained to the "warm boot". He wanted his program to be able to go back and start the new program when a certain key was pressed. He got this info through George Moses, who got it from his fishin' buddy, Jay (now Jamie) Fenton.

Just a little more trivia that roams around inside the head of Mike White.

I never understood the 24K on the Viper1 either, but the 8K in cart mode 
made sense to me.

The 24K switch just write protects the 16K of RAM in the VIPER. This prevents you from writing into the RAM area (hence the 8K mode). The 8k pertains to the 8K of cartridge space. The 24K pertains to the 8K of cartridge sapce and the 16K of RAM in the Viper.
Switching the A15 line instead of the A14 line makes a lot of sense to me because now you won't clobber the Utility, or in the case of Viper, the ViperSoft BASIC will be clobbered if you used the !6000 area.

I hope this makes some sort of sense to you. If you need more instructions, please let me know.
Ken

8540:
Two days ago (Feb. 22) I moved six items from the Misc. Section of Bally Alley to better places on the website.  At first I thought that this was going to be busy work, but it turns out that it isn't that AT ALL.  I've added better descriptions and I've read the documents- which has enlightened me.  In the early days of the Bally Alley website I didn't read EVERYTHING that went online (but I did skim it).  Now that I'm reading it, there are some true treasures (which I already knew, of course!).  If it wasn't for Mike White keeping good records of documentation, and sharing it, then much of this wouldn't have been previously available (although, I'm discovering that some of it is in "The Fabris Collection," but not ALL of it).  Here is what has been added:

1)  Moved the warranty card for Big City Slick and The Great American Jigsaw.  Not a big deal, but it fills in a gap.

2)  Moved the original (non-searchable) scan of the "Bally System Description."  This is by Cursor and is actually taken directly from the "Nutting Manual."  It's too bad that something like this wasn't included with each Bally Arcade / Astrocade.  It might have confused the heck out of beginners, but for those that could understand it, it would have proved very useful indeed.

3) Moved "Astrocade Programming Sheets." - These are programming sheets specifically for the Bally / Astrocade. These different sheets contain: BASIC Programming Pad, Z-80 Programmer's Pad, CX Value Screen Graph Paper, and Screen and Graphic Graph Paper.  Spectre is responsible for most, but not ALL, of these.  Thanks Brett!

4) Moved "Cartridge Making Instructions" - By Leroy Flamm.  Explains how to make a cartridge from a tape program.  Ken, is this pretty-much how you make your BASICarts?  I wonder if a way can be found to do this without the need to burn the EPROM on the Astrocade?  Perhaps Lance's new program would be of excellent use!

5) Moved "Bally On-Board ROM Subroutines" - Useful compilation of routines.  This booklet explains what the On-Board ROM routines built into the Bally / Astrocade ROM do.  This manual is used as a reference for BASIC programmers so that they can save a few bytes when programming and also take advantage of the faster routines that machine language offers.  A Hex dump of the Bally 8K ROM is also included (I wonder which ROM it is?).  After re-examining this document, I realize that the booklet that I found a few days ago by Tom Wood, created in 1978!, is nearly identical to this.  Tom really pulled up his sleeves and did some great disassembly of the ROM.  I'm going to have to look through some of the articles that he wrote for the Arcadian.  Paul, if you have any phone conversations that are labeled as "Tom Wood," I'd be interested in listening to them.

6) Moved "Crime Stopper Tips" - This article enables the programmer to use Hook Vectors to protect, as best possible, any software written in AstroBASIC from being copied, disassembled, etc.  I think using these hook vectors, it should be possible to make Critter work in AstroBASIC (as I don't think a version that works under this version of BASIC has been unearthed).

For links on where to download this documentation, check in the "What's New" section (under February 22'nd):

http://www.ballyalley.com/whats_new.html

Enjoy!

Adam

Section of Bally Alley to better places on the website.  At first I thought that this was going to be busy work, but it turns out that it isn't that AT ALL.  I've added better descriptions and I've read the documents- which has enlightened me.  In the early days of the Bally Alley website I didn't read EVERYTHING that went online (but I did skim it).  Now that I'm reading it, there are some true treasures (which I already knew, of course!).  If it wasn't for Mike White keeping good records of documentation, and sharing it, then much of this wouldn't have been previously available (although, I'm discovering that some of it is in "The Fabris Collection," but not ALL of it).  Here is what has been added:



1)  Moved the warranty card for Big City Slick and The Great American Jigsaw.  Not a big deal, but it fills in a gap.



2)  Moved the original (non-searchable) scan of the "Bally System Description. "  This is by Cursor and is actually taken directly from the "Nutting Manual."  It's too bad that something like this wasn't included with each Bally Arcade / Astrocade.  It might have confused the heck out of beginners, but for those that could understand it, it would have proved very useful indeed.



3) Moved "Astrocade Programming Sheets." - These are programming sheets specifically for the Bally / Astrocade. These different sheets contain: BASIC Programming Pad, Z-80 Programmer's Pad, CX Value Screen Graph Paper, and Screen and Graphic Graph Paper.  Spectre is responsible for most, but not ALL, of these.  Thanks Brett!



4) Moved "Cartridge Making Instructions" - By Leroy Flamm.  Explains how to make a cartridge from a tape program.  Ken, is this pretty-much how you make your BASICarts?  I wonder if a way can be found to do this without the need to burn the EPROM on the Astrocade?  Perhaps Lance's new program would be of excellent use!



5) Moved "Bally On-Board ROM Subroutines" - Useful compilation of routines.  This booklet explains what the On-Board ROM routines built into the Bally / Astrocade ROM do.  This manual is used as a reference for BASIC programmers so that they can save a few bytes when programming and also take advantage of the faster routines that machine language offers.  A Hex dump of the Bally 8K ROM is also included (I wonder which ROM it is?).  After re-examining this document, I realize that the booklet that I found a few days ago by Tom Wood, created in 1978!, is nearly identical to this.  Tom really pulled up his sleeves and did some great disassembly of the ROM.  I'm going to have to look through some of the articles that he wrote for the Arcadian.  Paul, if you have any phone conversations that are labeled as "Tom Wood," I'd be interested in listening to them.



6) Moved "Crime Stopper Tips" - This article enables the programmer to use Hook Vectors to protect, as best possible, any software written in AstroBASIC from being copied, disassembled, etc.  I think using these hook vectors, it should be possible to make Critter work in AstroBASIC (as I don't think a version that works under this version of BASIC has been unearthed).



For links on where to download this documentation, check in the "What's New" section (under February 22'nd):



http://www.ballyall ey.com/whats_ new.html



Enjoy!



Adam

The only direct mention of the Astrocade in the book (or bonus chapters)
that I can recall is on Page 192, in the Pac-Man chapter, when I include a
screenshot and caption for Ms. Candyman, below the same for the arcade
version of Mouse Trap. We do of course mention lots of Bally and Bally
Midway stuff, naturally, but that's all related to the arcade (naturally,
plenty of arcade conversions made it to the Astrocade, just not under their
original names).

As for the connection between "Game of Life" and "The Sims", it was mostly
about how you set the game's conditions and see how it plays out. In "Game
of Life", it's more about evolution and in "The Sims", it's more about
character development, though that of course is a form of evolution. The
major difference is that you have little control over "Game of Life" (in
fact, calling it a game in any form is a major stretch, it really is a
simulation) and a reasonable amount of control over "The Sims", with such
control varying depending upon what platform and what version you're
playing. While saying "The Sims" is a love it or hate it kind of game is a
stretch, I can see how someone doesn't like it (I'm by no means a huge fan).
A simplified and older form of "The Sims" can be found in "Alter Ego" (male
or female versions), which I'm more fond of (and can be played in a latter
day Web version), though again, Alter Ego is more of a "choose your own
adventure" format than any type of direct control.

They altered the original basic so that it doesn't check any keys. Then they made it so it didn't have to share the program with the screen, much like the extended BASICs. This gave them an entire 4K to save the program. If you look at any BALLY or ASTRO BASIC program through the Utility, you can't make any sense out of the program. But if you look at an extended BASIC, you can see the ASCII text. The program in this cart has this kind of text.
Ken

Q. Did you ever say, as has been widely circulated on the Internet, "640K [of RAM] ought to be enough for anybody?"

No! That makes me so mad I can't believe it! Do you realize the pain the industry went through while the IBM PC was limited to 640K? The machine was going to be 512K at one point, and we kept pushing it up. I never said that statement–I said the opposite of that.


I've read in other places, for quite a long time, that attributing a crazy quote to someone creditable is quite common.  I don't believe this quote. What you get if you subtract 85 from 255 four times is;
dec        binary        hex
255      1111 1111    FF
170      1010 1010    AA
  85      0101 0101    55

    0      0000 0000    00

You'll notice that by doing it this way, you check each bit with a 1 and a 0 twice. This is the quickest way to do a fairly thorough check.
You could do a bit-shift method, which is even better, but who wants to tie up their Bally all day?

8692:
There are three types of changes made to the BASIC in that cart...

First is by moving the pointers to the program text, which could
be done for any of the Basics, either into ROM or EXtended RAM.

Second, disabling the keypad - which is related to the first only
by the fact that you can not edit a program in ROM (it crashes.)
Done it two spots - WHATSU to check for pause while running, and
CHKIO to read the keypad (which jumps to RUN the program instead.)

Thirdly (and the reason the code got shifted) is that the version
of BALLY BASIC that they used had been edited to test out the new
"Graphic Line EDitor" using the PAUSE key (which showed up later.)

To do that they took out the ":RUN" routine completely, and broke
the ":INPUT" and ":LIST" also (but left the Calculator hooked in!)

Of course that feature (and tape reading) is useless in the DEMO,
but since it's different I posted the prototype as GLEDBBAS.BIN :

http://tech.groups.yahoo.com/group/ballyalley/files/GLEDBBAS.BIN

You had to use Word+Pause or Word+Space, but I took the liberty
of adding in the unshifted-Pause the way ASTRO BASIC had done it,
so it's that one byte different.  Did figure out that I was using
EDKEY wrong in the BALLY BASIC listing - should have been DEADKEY.

Balmisc Docsly (no extra '4' in there this time!!)

I added a preliminary version of source code for "Treasure Cove" that is ready to assemble... but it does NOT work.

This version assembles fine using Zmac, but it does NOT run.  When run under MESS .135, it "locks up."  When the debugger is used, the game is getting "stuck" in the WRITP routine in the system ROM.  The problem has been traced back to when the cartridge calls the WRITP routine from the cartridge area at $27DE.  The game never returns from this call.  Richard Degler suggests, "Sounds like the Stack area is getting clobbered by the WRITPattern - there is no bounds checking so if it draws too far down it just can't find its way back."

There are comments on the scanned source code, but none of them seem to pertain to this problem.  I've left the source code as it is.  If anyone is interested in looking at it for historical reasons, then it is available.  I'm not going to spend any time troubleshooting this code as there is a perfectly functional version of this in cartridge format... the cartridge dump of "Treasure Cove!"

I added the infamous undumped On-Board '3164' 8K Bally ROM.  This now makes for the third different archived ROM.

This ROM was dumped by Paul Thacker from his very early Bally Arcade console.  He comments about his system, "The system itself definitely seems early as well.  In addition to the different dust cover label, the red reset button, and the silver eject button, the casing is missing most of the explanatory text such as On/Off and 3/4 for the channel."

Richard Degler took a look at this ROM and has some comments, "Differences from the "3159" BIOS are the SYSTEM Routine Jump Table (since the routines are shifted), and the location of text strings and the Font (which is why to use the Dope Vector). The date starts at 3604 and is the leftover "977" of WHITE BIOS. After that the built-in games have few changes, except Gunfight plays to 9999 (like the 1978 version) and has one color changed. CHECKSUMs #1 and 2, as well as FUDGE4 are also different, so the un-modified BAL-CHECK should work fine on this machine as it is."

I've added Richard's recent update of the Bally ROM source code.  Here is a description of all the Bally ROM source code available on the website.

The Bally ROM scans from the "Nutting Manual" and the code in ready-to-assemble format are both available.  Both include the source for the 4K of System ROM, and the other 4K contain Checkmate, Calculator, Gun Fight and Scribble.

The scans of the manual are not needed anymore now that the source-code has been retyped.  It is for archival and reference purposes.  The "archive" version of the source code assembles to the 8K Bally On-board ROM.  It matches EXACTLY with the 3159 version.  This version matches VERY closely with the scanned "Nutting Manual" source code, so it is being kept for reference.

The "gold standard" version, created and updated by Richard Degler, is the updated assembly source code for ALL THREE versions of the Bally System BIOS.  It can be used to recreate any version of the on-board ROMs.  By changing the EQUate 0,1s in the first block marked with "###"'s you can conditionally generate _either_ the WHITE.bin or ASTRO.bin (a.k.a BIOS3159.BIN or "GAME OVER" ROM) from the same source code.

I have added three tools for 300-BAUD archiving to BallyAlley.com.  Ronaldo Goulart has put this great collection of archiving tools together.  Thanks for all the work!  Here is what is included:

1) KCS

     KCS allows the user to create binary dumps from wave recordings, and to convert such dumps back to wave. It is a DOS application, programmed in a custom Forth dialect, DX-Forth, but it's author kindly provided me with a version adapted for a Windows Forth interpreter, so both a DOS and a Windows version are available. The Windows executable is much bigger because of the additional runtimes embedded in the executable.
      For converting .prg binary dumps back to wave using KCS, a known-working, though not optimal set of command line switches is " -M -L5 -P50". Refer to KCS documentation for further details.

2) Prg2txt:

     prg2txt is a Windows utility for converting binary dumps of Bally Basic / ViperSoft Basic into Unicode text files. By default, it produces an output similar to the regular original listings, and through an optional command line switch, it generates the output file using an alternative syntax, intended to allow the listing to be edited through a regular plain text editor. Such listings can be converted back to binary using txt2prg.

3) txt2prg:
     txt2prg generates binary files from text listings, which can after be converted to wave for loading into an original Astrocade. In case you are going to edit your own listings or the ones generated using prg2txt, be sure to use the special required syntax. For more information on this, refer to txt2prg.txt.

I added a dissassembler script for DZ80, version 2.00.  This script was created by Richard Degler in August of 2009.  Here are Richard's full comments:


It took me all weekend but it works great!  No more adjusting garbage code
following RST $38 syssuk'ed routines!!  Here's my Bally HVG LUA script.zip
 
LUA is like a pre-ANSI C so I was banging my head a lot.  It didn't even
have a % or MODulo operator, which made things difficult.  Not everything
mentioned on their website was included, and the error reporting is awful.
 
Didn't test it with dZ80 1.50 but you can get 2.00 (from 2002) at :
http://www.inkland.org.uk/dz80 - they let http://www.inkland.org lapse
 
Just enable script at bottom of Options and Browse to BALLYHVG.LUA then
dis-assemble a Bally game ROM and see it actually disassemble HVG code.
 
I don't like the lower-case labels, they confuse me (and Zmac 1.3, too?)
and you still have to type in the Start and Ending addresses (in DECIMAL)
then the start in AGAIN as File Start, instead of just the ORGin offset.
 
One caveat, if you want to leave the Hex as a 'h' suffix it will still
show the DW's with a '$' prefix.  Would have made it conditional, but not
sure how to duplicate their '{' to put leading 0's before A to F digits.
 
It did get confused by $FF as the last byte of a file, said it was a NOP.


There aren't many people disassembling Astrocade cartridges, but for those that ARE (or plan to?), then this script is just what you've been looking for!

You can download it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_tools/Bally_HVG_LUA_script.zip

Okay, for those that want practice, go ahead and disassemble a game.  How about... "Galactic Invasion" or "The Incredible Wizard?"  ;-)

Have fun!

You quoted my mis-type without making the correction I posted two messages later - it was the BIOS3164.BIN called "GAME OVER" ROM
(the number is the address of that string.)  So it should say ...
"
conditionally generate _either_ the WHITE.bin or ASTRO.bin (a.k.a
BIOS3159.BIN) both known as "OVER" ROMs, in addition to version 0 BALLY.bin (BIOS3164.BIN or "GAME OVER") from the same source code.
/"

Here's a timeline of the mis-alignment at the end of system code
(where '.' is really a NULL or 0 byte and 'f's are $FFs or -1's) :

BALLY [3164] ==> (C) BALLY MFG 1977. (in earliest Bally H.L.C.'s)

WHITE [3159] ==> BALLY MFG 1977.977. (branded from Motgomery Ward)

ASTRO [3159] ==> BALLY MFG 1978.ffff (in most BPAs and Astrocades)

starting at $0E06 going up to $0E18 (or in decimal 3590 thru 3608)
after which SCRIBBLE aligns. Wish we had accurate dates for these.


BTW "Preview" in the Group Editor is what puts blank lines on top.

Richard

The date starts at 3604 and is the leftover "977" of WHITE BIOS. After that the built-in games have few changes, except Gunfight plays to 9999 (like the 1978 version) and has one color changed. CHECKSUMs #1 and 2, as well as FUDGE4 are also different, so the un-modified BAL-CHECK should work fine on this machine as it is."
